$comment: Shared conformance corpus for the SQL validator.
The Python implementation (pipeline/guardrails.py) and the TypeScript one
(web/lib/guardrails) are both tested against this file. Two implementations
of the same rules will drift unless something forces them to agree; this is
'codes' lists violation codes that MUST be present on a denial. A denial may
report additional codes - a query can be wrong in more than one way - but it

cases.why: The ordinary case has to keep working.
cases.sql: SELECT sector, COUNT(*) AS n FROM crm_accounts GROUP BY sector LIMIT 50
SELECT a.sector, AVG(CASE WHEN o.is_won THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS win_rate FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN crm_accounts a ON a.account = o.account WHERE o.is_closed GROUP BY a.sector

cases.why: Common table expressions are normal analytical SQL, and their names must not be mistaken for unknown tables.
cases.sql: WITH live AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_status <> 'canceled') SELECT COUNT(*) FROM live

cases.why: A limit the model is asked to include is a limit it will sometimes forget, so the validator adds one.
A model can ask for a million rows. It does not get them.
Clamping must not raise a limit the model set deliberately.

The classic injection shape: a valid query followed by a second one. Both validators report not_select rather than a statement count: DuckDB refuses to serialise a batch containing a non-SELECT and never reveals how many statements it held, so the Python side checks statement type first to match.
cases.sql: SELECT 1 FROM orders; DROP TABLE orders

cases.why: A keyword blocklist is defeated by a comment. An AST is not. Both validators report not_select rather than a statement count: DuckDB refuses to serialise a batch containing a non-SELECT and never reveals how many statements it held, so the Python side checks statement type first to match.
cases.sql:
SELECT 1 FROM orders; -- harmless
DROP TABLE customers

cases.why: Case folding must not change the verdict.
A hallucinated table is the single most common text-to-SQL failure.
A hallucinated column on a real table is the second most common.
Syntactically fine, semantically meaningless: a synthetic hardware vendor joined to a real marketplace.
cases.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM crm_opportunities o JOIN deal_outcomes d ON o.account = d.seller_id

cases.why: Two 99,000-row tables with no ON clause is a hung browser tab, not a slow query.
The views are built on read_parquet; the model must not call it directly.
Models sometimes answer in prose when they should emit SQL.
cases.sql: I cannot answer that question with the available data.

cases.why: A UNION is a place to smuggle a second source past a check that only looks at the first.
cases.sql: SELECT order_id FROM orders UNION ALL SELECT id FROM secret_table

cases.why: Nesting must not hide a table from the check.
cases.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM internal_payroll) AS x LIMIT 5
